deep.reconstruction:
Context: the previous page tabulates [1000/k] for k=1..33, i.e. up to about sqrt(1000). This is the data for a hyperbola-type evaluation of sum [n/k]. The next page studies second differences [n/s]-2[n/(s+1)]+[n/(s+2)] and fractional parts, apparently looking for a cheap way to sum the [n/k] for large k. This page sits between them and sets up the counting framework.

(A) Asymptotics of power sums (top of page).
(1) Riemann sum: int_0^1 x^alpha dx = lim (1/n) sum_{s=0}^{n-1} (s/n)^alpha. Written as an identity, the limit is understood. The marginal '1/n | 1/n^alpha' records the step 1/n and the factor 1/n^alpha.
(2) Hence n^{-(1+alpha)}(1+2^alpha+...+(n-1)^alpha) -> 1/(alpha+1).
(3) Replacing alpha by -alpha (0<alpha<1): 1+2^{-alpha}+...+(n-1)^{-alpha} ~ n^{1-alpha}/(1-alpha).
(4) A partly stain-covered line. I read it as n^alpha(1+2^{-alpha}+...+n^{-alpha}) ~ n/(1-alpha), i.e. sum_{k<=n}(n/k)^alpha ~ n/(1-alpha); the exponent alpha on n is my reading. This is the smooth analogue of sum_k [n/k]; as alpha -> 1 it degenerates into n log n.

(B) Lattice-point counts.
- The conditions a<=n, ab<=n, abc<=n define
  n_2 = sum_a [n/a] = #{(a,b): ab<=n} (the Dirichlet divisor sum D(n)), and
  n_3 = sum [n/(ab)] = #{(a,b,c): abc<=n}.
- '[n/a] = alpha' names the number of admissible b for a given a. The line 'sum[c/b]' is partly illegible.
- 'a partir de 2' (starting from 2): Riemann then restricts all factors to be >= 2. So n_k = #{(a_1,...,a_k): a_i>=2, a_1...a_k<=n}.
  - n_1 = n-1 (the integers 2..n). The manuscript seems to read n-2; see errors.
  - n_2 = sum_{a>=2}([n/a]-1), left blank on the page.

(C) Key formula: s_1 = n_1 - n_2/2 + n_3/3 - n_4/4 + ...
Implicit derivation (mine):
- log zeta(s) = log(1+(zeta(s)-1)) = sum_k (-1)^{k+1}(zeta(s)-1)^k/k.
- (zeta(s)-1)^k = sum_m d'_k(m) m^{-s}, where d'_k(m) counts ordered factorizations of m into k factors >= 2.
- Summing coefficients up to n gives s_1 = sum_k (-1)^{k+1} n_k/k.
- Since log zeta(s) = sum_p sum_m p^{-ms}/m, this s_1 equals Riemann's 1859 function f(n) = sum_{p^m<=n} 1/m = pi(n) + pi(n^{1/2})/2 + pi(n^{1/3})/3 + ...
This is an elementary, purely combinatorial formula for f(n), and hence for pi(n) by Moebius inversion, in terms of hyperbolic lattice-point counts. In modern terms it is Linnik's identity. The line '1,2,3,...,n  [n/a], n' refers to these counts.

(D) Variant: log(1+2^{-s}+3^{-s}+...) - log(1+2^{-2s}+3^{-2s}+...) = log(zeta(s)/zeta(2s)) = sum_p log(1+p^{-s}) = sum_p sum_m (-1)^{m+1} p^{-ms}/m.
- The coefficient sum gives pi(n) - pi(n^{1/2})/2 + pi(n^{1/3})/3 - ...
- Equivalently, it can be expanded via the squarefree series zeta(s)/zeta(2s) = sum |mu(n)| n^{-s}.
- This is presumably an alternative with faster-dying higher terms.

(E) Short intervals.
- The line [n/1]+[n/2]+[n/3]+... restates n_2.
- The conditions m<ab<n, m<abc<n, m<abcd<n, with ranges [m/a] < b < [n/a] and [m/(ab)] < c < [n/(ab)], set up the differences n_k(n)-n_k(m).
- This would count primes (via f) in an interval (m,n) by nested summation over the first factors.

Overall: a plan to compute f(x), hence pi(x), by counting lattice points under hyperbolas, with numerical work for n=1000 (previous page) and n=10000 (next page).
errors: The '=' signs in (2)-(4) denote limits or asymptotic equality, not exact identities.
In (3), n^{1-alpha}/(1-alpha) is only the leading term, valid for 0<alpha<1. The partial sum is n^{1-alpha}/(1-alpha) + zeta(alpha) + o(1).
n_1 is transcribed 'n-2'. Counting integers from 2 to n gives n-1, so either a slip or a misreading.
The line under the stain (n^alpha(...) = n/(1-alpha)) is partly illegible. The reconstruction n^alpha sum_{k<=n} k^{-alpha} ~ n/(1-alpha) is correct as an asymptotic.
No error in the central formula s_1 = sum (-1)^{k+1} n_k/k. It is exact, a finite sum since n_k = 0 for 2^k > n.

results.what: Riemann-sum asymptotics: sum_{k<n} k^alpha ~ n^{1+alpha}/(1+alpha) and sum_{k<n} k^{-alpha} ~ n^{1-alpha}/(1-alpha)
n_2 = sum [n/a] counts lattice points under ab<=n; n_3 = sum [n/(ab)] counts triples
results.modern_name: Dirichlet divisor summatory function D(n), D_3(n); hyperbola method

results.what: f(n) = sum_{p^m<=n} 1/m = sum_k (-1)^{k+1} n_k/k, with n_k the number of ordered k-tuples of integers >=2 with product <=n, derived from log zeta = log(1+(zeta-1))
results.modern_name: Linnik's identity (Lambda(n)/log n = sum_k (-1)^{k-1} d'_k(n)/k), summed form
results.usually_credited_to: Yu. V. Linnik (1961); later used in Heath-Brown-type identities and combinatorial pi(x) algorithms

results.what: log zeta(s) - log zeta(2s) = sum_p log(1+p^{-s}), giving pi(n) - pi(n^{1/2})/2 + pi(n^{1/3})/3 - ...
results.modern_name: Euler product of zeta(s)/zeta(2s) (squarefree generating function)

results.what: Counting k-fold products in an interval (m,n) by nested ranges [m/a] < b < [n/a], etc.
results.modern_name: short-interval lattice-point counting for prime counting
results.usually_credited_to: cf. Meissel-Lehmer style combinatorial methods (19th-20th c.)

deep.surprise_reason: Riemann's f(x) and log zeta are his own. However, explicitly using log(1+(zeta-1)) to express f(n) exactly as an alternating sum of hyperbolic lattice-point counts n_k/k is what is now called Linnik's identity (1961). Combined with actual numerical work on [1000/k] and [10000/k], this looks like an unpublished elementary algorithm for pi(x). It is a natural step from his 1859 setup, so notable but not revolutionary.
